summary: Twenty-two EuroPLoP 2026 attendees discussed, for 90 minutes, what stays human when agents draft architecture. The report's own conclusion is that decision ownership, accountability, and human-written guardrails were the shared themes, with criticality as the knob for oversight, and that 'harness engineering' and 'cognitive debt' were names the room used. Those are interpretations of one plenary, not counted votes or observed outcomes, and the authors say a real qualitative analysis is still planned.

claims.claim: There was broad consensus that architectural decision-making, accountability, and the authoring of guardrails remain human tasks.
claims.evidence: Section 4.3 quotes individual speakers and calls the agreement strong. There is no vote, no count of dissent, and speaker turns were not attributed. Nineteen of 22 people spoke, in a 90-minute plenary the authors say was larger than a normal focus group. Section 6.4 says this is the authors' synthesis, not a formal coding.

claims.claim: Criticality, defined as uncertainty combined with cost of change, is the universal criterion for how much human oversight AI work needs.
claims.evidence: Section 5.1: one participant's framing 'was accepted by the group without dissent'. No other operationalization is tested. Section 5.3 lists unresolved tensions (skill versus speed, understanding versus bounded risk) that the same slogan is then asked to settle.

claims.claim: Harness engineering emerged as a new discipline: the system that governs AI-assisted system creation, including validation, a knowledge layer, and company standards.
claims.evidence: Section 4.4: one participant introduced the term and others extended it. Section 6.2 says that origin explicitly. The logistics-company modernization story in the same section is labeled unverified. Section 5.2's definition is the authors'. External mining papers are cited as related practice, not as results of this session. Participants also said nobody knows how to assess harness quality except by looking at outputs.

claims.claim: Cognitive debt is a systemic risk: three mechanisms erode architects' understanding when they accept AI proposals without full engagement.
claims.evidence: Section 4.3 records the term from a participant, by analogy with technical debt. Section 5.1 says the three mechanisms (shallow acceptance, brief engagement, fly-by approval) are the authors' extension. No observation of later architectural mistakes is reported.

claims.claim: Existing validation (CI, tests, static analysis) is still the right quality backbone for AI-written code.
claims.evidence: Section 4.2 quotes one participant that a SonarQube harness is the same distrust used for human code, and reports group agreement. No defect data. This sits next to the claim that a new harness layer is required and that its quality cannot be judged from outputs.

patterns.note: Several participants said a one-line prompt makes the agent assume the wrong design, and that they start from a detailed implementation plan (§4.1). Others said they still hand-write the first feature slices so later agent code has a style to copy. No comparison of plan-first versus prompt-first work was made.

The room's stated rule is that a named human accepts the architecture decision and the production change (§4.3, §4.5). The same session described fly-by approval, where frequent agent confirmations are clicked through. The report does not measure whether gates are exercised or rubber-stamped.

One participant described a rules document that humans alone may edit and that is given to the agent as fixed background (§4.3). The harness shopping list (LLM-agnostic instructions, company standards, mixed deterministic and model checks) is discussion, not a tested policy.

Architecture decision records are described as memory for agents that otherwise forget across sessions, and the harness is said to need a knowledge layer of company standards (§4.1, §4.4). No record format is compared with another, and no agent is run.

Cognitive debt and the aviation autopilot analogy are the session's learning concern: people who stop doing the work lose the skill, and juniors ask a model instead of a senior (§4.3, §4.6). The education consensus (keep fundamentals, add specification and harness skills, drop some language breadth) is opinion from this room.

Uses mentioned include gathering context for agents, reverse-engineering legacy architecture, and exploring an unfamiliar stack before implementation (§4.1). The session did not compare discovery-before-spec with specifying from memory.
Participants said unit tests, end-to-end tests, and static analysis still apply to agent output (§4.2). That is a preference, not a result about whether those checks catch architectural mistakes.

methodology.sample: 22 volunteers at EuroPLoP 2026 (Irsee, July 2026) plus three researchers. Questionnaire returned by 18: 12 academic and 6 industry roles; development experience median 14 years; architecture experience median 5 years; self-rated architecture from novice (1) to expert (1). Session length 90 minutes. Nineteen people spoke.
methodology.baselines: None. Three earlier interviews shaped the guide and are not reported.
methodology.models: None run. Self-reported tools among 18 respondents: ChatGPT 14, Claude 13, GitHub Copilot 8, Cursor 3. Most rated themselves intermediate or novice AI users.
methodology.variance: Not applicable. No claim counts, inter-rater statistics, or vote tallies. Member check by 5 self-selected participants.
methodology.contamination_controls: Not applicable. The guide was pre-structured from three interviews, which the authors note can hide topics those interviews missed.
methodology.languages: Not a code study. Reported system types among respondents include web/cloud (13), distributed (7), data-intensive (7), enterprise (7), and embedded (6). Team sizes mostly under 15.

standards.peer_review: Authors' accepted manuscript for EuroPLoP 2026, to appear in Springer LNCS. The arXiv comment says 21 pages, EuroPLoP 2026. This is not the version of record. The paper itself calls the text an experience report and says a formal thematic analysis is future work.
standards.artifacts: No transcript, questionnaire microdata, or codebook. Local transcription with faster-whisper is described. Quotes were edited for readability.

biases.detail: Volunteers at a patterns conference. The authors say the room is architecture-aware and not the broader developer population. Six of 18 questionnaire respondents were from industry. AI-tool expertise was mostly intermediate or novice.
One 90-minute plenary of 22 people. Parts C and D crowded out autonomy and education. Individual turns were short.
People who attend EuroPLoP and stay for this session are already reflective about design practice. Quiet or skeptical practitioners are under-represented; five member-checkers opted in.

The close quotes a participant that software development is dead and harness engineering lives on. The logistics rewrite that 'was considered impossible' is explicitly unverified. Section 7 still leads with consensus language the methods section will not support.

Harness engineering is presented as a new discipline. The paper also cites an existing essay that uses the term, plus architectural fitness functions and executable architecture rules, and then distinguishes the harness mainly by definition.
Tool use and experience are a voluntary 18-person questionnaire. Practice claims (ADR quality, specification skill, production fear) are uncheckable anecdotes.

coi.affiliations: Uwe van Heesch and Christian Kohls, TH Köln; Olaf Zimmermann, University of St.Gallen.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: No system is evaluated. Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Kiro, SonarQube, ArchUnit, and Lovable are examples in the discussion.
coi.funding: Olaf Zimmermann acknowledges Swiss National Science Foundation grant 10002384 (TaSSAreCt). No industry sponsor is named.
coi.detail: The facilitators' prior work (architecture decision records, and van Heesch's essay that the practiced craft no longer exists) frames the session, and section 6.4 admits the moderator's questions shaped it. They do not score a product they sell. The harness theme was introduced by a participant and then formalized by the authors.

verdict_reason: A careful experience report of one expert plenary: demographics are counted, the analysis limits are stated, and an unverified success story is marked unverified. The findings the abstract calls consensus and a universal criterion are uncounted interpretations, the harness term came from one speaker, cognitive debt's three mechanisms are the authors' gloss, and a formal coding is explicitly future work. Useful as a map of practitioner worries for harness design, not as evidence that those practices work.
applicability: Directly about the decisions this Java multi-repo team has to make, and only as practitioner opinion. The relevant worries are: keep architectural choices and the guardrail text human-authored; treat criticality (how unsure the change is, and how expensive it is to undo across the ingestion repositories) as the reason to require a person; expect decision records to be read by agents as well as people; and do not equate a green build with a good harness, because the room said harness quality is only visible indirectly. Cognitive debt matches a rollout risk for new developers who accept agent diffs in healthcare-education code they do not yet understand. The sample is a patterns conference, mostly academic, mostly small teams, not a measured Java estate. Nothing here tests spec-first development, and the closing slogan that software development is over should not drive the rollout.

conflicts_with.detail: That position paper claims human review's marginal benefit no longer justifies its cost, while carving out regulated work that needs a named accountable person. This focus group reports the opposite default: the same validation distrust used for human code still applies, and a human remains accountable for agent output. Both are opinion. This session also describes fly-by approval, which is the failure mode that would make a human gate cheap and empty.

That workshop roadmap says current processes cannot simply host agents and that each adopted process must be redesigned from an AI-first perspective. This report's participants say the quality backbone does not change: existing tests and static analysis are the right distrust for agent code. One is a call to rebuild the process; the other is a call to keep the existing checks and put new effort into human-written constraints.
